document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a 3-year history of peptic ulcer disease develops sudden severe generalized abdominal pain while at work. On arrival he lies motionless. Temperature is 37.8°C, heart rate 112 bpm. The abdomen is rigid with diffuse guarding and absent bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the most common presentations of surgical pain: sudden onset with a rigid abdomen indicates a perforated viscus, pain out of proportion to physical findings indicates ischemic bowel, vague pain that later localizes suggests appendicitis, and waves of colicky pain suggest bowel obstruction. This man's abrupt onset of pain with board-like rigidity and diffuse guarding fits perforation, and his ulcer history provides the likely source.

optionExplanations.b: Bowel obstruction produces waves of colicky pain with distention rather than sudden onset rigidity.
optionExplanations.c: Pancreatitis can mimic a surgical abdomen but is rarely an indication for immediate surgery and characteristically radiates to the back.
optionExplanations.d: Ischemic bowel is characterised by pain out of proportion to physical findings, with minimal peritoneal signs early on.
optionExplanations.e: Appendicitis classically begins as vague periumbilical pain that subsequently localises, not instantaneous diffuse rigidity.

source.reference: GS5 — Differential Diagnosis of Acute Abdominal Pain / Most Common Presentations of Surgical Pain

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is booked for an elective open sigmoid colectomy for recurrent diverticulitis. She has no drug allergies. The surgical team is completing the preoperative checklist and asks about antimicrobial prophylaxis. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic antibiotic strategy for this operation?

options.text: Cefazolin plus metronidazole given within 1 hour before skin incision
Cefazolin given at the time of skin closure
Oral ciprofloxacin started 24 hours before the operation
No antibiotic prophylaxis, with antibiotics reserved for postoperative fever

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that prophylactic antibiotics are chosen by wound class and given immediately or within 1 hour before incision: cefazolin for skin flora, with metronidazole added for GI flora coverage in contaminated cases. Colorectal resection entails entry into a hollow viscus, so combined skin and GI flora coverage timed to incision is appropriate; postoperative antibiotics are reserved for suspected or documented intra-abdominal infection.

optionExplanations.b: Prophylaxis must be in the tissues at the time of incision; giving it at closure forfeits the benefit.
optionExplanations.c: Prolonged preoperative oral antibiotics are not the recommended prophylactic regimen and prolonged preoperative hospitalisation and multiple antibiotics are themselves risk factors for infection.
optionExplanations.d: Prophylaxis is recommended for most surgeries; only low-risk clean procedures such as elective thyroidectomy or hemorrhoidectomy may omit it.
optionExplanations.e: Postoperative antibiotics are reserved for treatment of suspected or documented intra-abdominal infection, not routine prophylaxis.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast found on screening mammography. The axilla is clinically and sonographically normal, the tumour is unifocal, and she has no contraindication to radiation. She wishes to keep her breast if oncologically safe. What is the most appropriate primary surgical management?

options.text: Breast conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy, followed by radiotherapy
Modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection
Breast conserving surgery with axillary lymph node dissection and no radiotherapy
Radical mastectomy removing pectoralis muscle and axillary nodes

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that breast conserving surgery can be offered to most women with stage I/II disease and that there is no survival benefit of mastectomy over lumpectomy plus radiation for stage I and II disease, provided lumpectomy is combined with radiation. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is performed in women with clinically node-negative invasive breast cancer. This unifocal, node-negative T1 tumour therefore fits breast conservation with sentinel node biopsy and adjuvant radiotherapy.

optionExplanations.b: Modified radical mastectomy with full axillary dissection is not required for a small clinically node-negative tumour and offers no survival advantage.
optionExplanations.c: Omitting axillary staging in invasive cancer forfeits pathologic nodal information needed for staging and adjuvant decisions.
optionExplanations.d: Lumpectomy must be combined with radiation for survival equivalent to mastectomy, and full axillary dissection is unnecessary when the axilla is clinically negative.
optionExplanations.e: Radical mastectomy is now rarely performed and is far more morbid than the disease requires here.

source.reference: GS69 — Breast Cancer Treatment / Primary Surgical Treatment

questions.question: A 52-year-old lifelong non-smoker has a CT abdomen for flank pain that incidentally shows a single 7 mm solid pulmonary nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth borders. She has no cancer history and no other risk factors for lung cancer. No prior chest imaging is available. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat CT chest at 6-12 months, then consider CT at 18-24 months
No further imaging follow-up is required
CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy of the nodule
Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of the nodule

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes reproduces the Fleischner Society approach to solid nodules: a single solid nodule under 6 mm in a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up, a 6-8 mm nodule warrants CT at 6-12 months then consideration of CT at 18-24 months, and a nodule larger than 8 mm prompts CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling. This 7 mm solid nodule in a low-risk patient therefore falls into the 6-8 mm surveillance category.

optionExplanations.b: No routine follow-up applies only to single solid nodules smaller than 6 mm in low-risk patients.
optionExplanations.c: PET/CT is reserved for nodules larger than 8 mm, where it helps narrow the differential.
optionExplanations.d: Biopsy is indicated when clinical and radiographic features cannot distinguish benign from malignant, or in patients at risk for lung cancer, neither of which applies here.
optionExplanations.e: Surgical excision is disproportionate for a small smooth-bordered nodule in a low-risk patient.

source.reference: GS14 — Solitary Pulmonary Nodule / Evaluation of a Solitary Pulmonary Nodule

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history presents with cough and weight loss. Serum sodium is 118 mmol/L with concentrated urine and euvolemia, consistent with SIADH. CT chest shows a large central hilar mass with bulky mediastinal adenopathy. Which malignancy is the most likely cause of his presentation?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Large cell carcinoma of the lung

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes tabulates paraneoplastic syndromes by associated malignancy: SIADH and Lambert-Eaton syndrome are linked with small cell lung cancer, hypercalcemia from osteolysis or PTHrP and hypophosphatemia with squamous cell carcinoma, Cushing's syndrome from ACTH and carcinoid syndrome with bronchial carcinoid, and clubbing with hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy with non-small cell lung cancer. Hyponatremia from SIADH in a heavy smoker with a central mass therefore points to small cell lung cancer.

optionExplanations.b: Squamous cell carcinoma is the classic cause of paraneoplastic hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia rather than SIADH.
optionExplanations.c: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and is not the lung tumour listed with SIADH.
optionExplanations.d: Bronchial carcinoid is associated with Cushing's syndrome from ectopic ACTH and with carcinoid syndrome.
optionExplanations.e: Large cell carcinoma is a non-small cell subtype and is not the tumour associated with SIADH in this table.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman reports 4 months of fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and fatigable proximal weakness that worsens through the day. A CT chest performed for dyspnea demonstrates a well-circumscribed 5 cm mass in the anterior mediastinum, anterior to the pericardium and great vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes notes that mediastinal masses are diagnosed by compartment and age, that the anterior compartment differential is the four Ts (thymoma, thyroid enlargement, teratoma, tumours), and that paraneoplastic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis accompany thymomas. Thymomas are rare anterior mediastinal neoplasms of patients aged 40-60 with a strong association with myasthenia gravis, matching this presentation.

optionExplanations.b: Bronchogenic cysts are middle compartment lesions and are not associated with myasthenia gravis.
optionExplanations.c: Neurogenic tumours arise in the posterior compartment and are evaluated with MRI.
optionExplanations.d: Pericardial cysts occupy the anterior or middle compartment but do not cause fatigable weakness.
optionExplanations.e: Esophageal tumours are posterior compartment lesions and typically present with dysphagia.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man develops excruciating retrosternal and neck pain immediately after an episode of repeated forceful vomiting following a large meal. Temperature is 38.4°C, heart rate 118 bpm. There is crepitus in the neck, and chest x-ray shows pneumomediastinum with a small left pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Dilute barium contrast esophagram as the initial study

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists Boerhaave's syndrome as a barogenic transmural esophageal perforation caused by repeated forceful vomiting, presenting with chest or neck pain, fever, tachycardia, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and pleural effusion. For confirmation, a Gastrografin (water-soluble contrast) upper GI study is the first choice, followed by a dilute barium study if the water-soluble study is negative.

optionExplanations.b: Dilute barium is the second-line study performed only after a negative water-soluble contrast examination.
optionExplanations.c: Endoscopy is itself the most common iatrogenic cause of perforation and is not the recommended confirmatory test here.
optionExplanations.d: Transesophageal echocardiography assesses cardiac structures and risks further esophageal injury.
optionExplanations.e: MRI is not among the listed investigations for suspected esophageal perforation.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with long-standing duodenal ulcer disease reports 6 weeks of crampy epigastric pain and vomiting of large volumes of undigested, non-bilious food. He has lost 8 kg. On examination the epigastrium is distended and a splashing noise is heard with the stethoscope when the patient is rocked. Which complication of duodenal ulceration best explains this picture?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes gastric outlet obstruction as a complication in which ulceration produces edema and fibrosis of the pyloric channel, causing non-bilious vomiting of undigested food, a dilated stomach, crampy abdominal pain, and a succussion splash heard over the stomach when the patient is shaken. This patient's succussion splash with retained undigested food is characteristic.

optionExplanations.b: Perforation presents with sudden pain and a rigid, diffusely guarded abdomen with free air under the diaphragm.
optionExplanations.c: Penetration causes constant mid-epigastric pain burrowing into the back, unrelated to meals, with elevated amylase or lipase.
optionExplanations.d: Gastroduodenal artery involvement causes hemorrhage with hematemesis or melena rather than retained food.
optionExplanations.e: Gastric carcinoma is a separate entity that presents insidiously with anorexia and weight loss rather than a classic succussion splash from pyloric channel scarring.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman with previous appendectomy and hysterectomy presents with 18 hours of colicky periumbilical pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, and inability to pass flatus. She is afebrile with a normal white cell count and lactate, and the abdomen is soft with no localized tenderness. CT shows a transition point with proximal dilated bowel and no features of ischemia. What is the best initial management?

options.text: NPO, IV isotonic fluid resuscitation, and nasogastric tube decompression with serial reassessment
Barium enema to define the level of obstruction
Start a clear fluid diet and oral laxatives
Urgent colonoscopy to decompress the bowel

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes advises that with no clinical features of ischemia, small bowel obstruction is managed with a short course of conservative therapy: IV isotonic fluid resuscitation with urine output monitoring, NPO, and nasogastric decompression with frequent re-examination by the surgical team. Adhesional obstruction in a patient with previous abdominal surgery resolves spontaneously with nasogastric decompression about 70% of the time; surgery follows if the obstruction fails to resolve or ischemia develops.

optionExplanations.b: Immediate operation is reserved for suspected ischemia, necrosis or perforation, or for a patient with no prior abdominal surgery.
optionExplanations.c: CT with IV contrast is first line; barium enema is not the recommended study for suspected small bowel obstruction.
optionExplanations.d: Oral intake worsens distention and vomiting; the patient should be kept NPO.
optionExplanations.e: Colonoscopy addresses colonic pathology and does not decompress a mechanical small bowel obstruction.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped his anticoagulant presents with 5 hours of severe periumbilical pain, vomiting, and one episode of bloody diarrhea. He is writhing in pain yet the abdomen is soft with only minimal tenderness and no peritoneal signs. Lactate is elevated. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler of the portal vein

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that acute intestinal ischemia presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, and minimal early peritoneal signs, and that CT angiography is the gold standard for acute arterial mesenteric ischemia. This embolic presentation in a patient with untreated atrial fibrillation therefore warrants CT angiography.

optionExplanations.b: Ultrasound is not listed as the diagnostic modality for acute arterial mesenteric ischemia.
optionExplanations.c: Plain films may show portal venous gas, pneumatosis, or free air, but these are late findings and would delay diagnosis.
optionExplanations.d: Colonoscopy is not the investigation of choice in suspected acute arterial mesenteric ischemia and risks perforation of ischemic bowel.
optionExplanations.e: MRCP evaluates the biliary and pancreatic ducts and has no role here.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man undergoes repair of a right groin hernia that has intermittently descended into the scrotum since adolescence. At operation the hernia sac is found to originate at the deep inguinal ring and lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery as it enters the inguinal canal. What is the most likely type of hernia?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes uses the mnemonic MD's don't LIe: a hernia medial to the inferior epigastric artery is direct, while one lateral to the inferior epigastric artery is indirect. Indirect hernias arise from congenital persistence of the processus vaginalis, originate at the deep inguinal ring, and often descend into the scrotum, which matches this patient's long-standing scrotal hernia found lateral to the vessels.

optionExplanations.b: A direct hernia passes through Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery and usually does not descend into the scrotal sac.
optionExplanations.c: A femoral hernia enters the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, not the deep inguinal ring.
optionExplanations.d: Obturator hernias are internal hernias that require CT for diagnosis and are not encountered at the deep inguinal ring.
optionExplanations.e: Incisional hernias arise through a previous fascial closure, not through the inguinal canal.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman who has had four pregnancies presents with a tender 2 cm lump in the right groin. On examination the mass lies below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein, and it does not descend toward the labia. She has no prior groin surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes femoral hernias as affecting mostly females, arising from pregnancy-related weakness of the pelvic floor musculature and raised intra-abdominal pressure, and passing into the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, lying medial to the femoral vein. This patient's parity and the location of the mass below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein identify a femoral hernia.

optionExplanations.b: An indirect inguinal hernia originates at the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric artery and often descends into the labia majora.
optionExplanations.c: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through Hesselbach's triangle above the inguinal ligament.
optionExplanations.d: An incisional hernia requires a previous abdominal wall incision, which she does not have.
optionExplanations.e: An umbilical hernia presents at the umbilicus, not in the groin.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man has had 5 days of right lower quadrant pain and fever. He is hemodynamically stable with a tender right lower quadrant fullness. CT demonstrates a perforated appendix with a well-defined 6 cm rim-enhancing periappendiceal abscess and no free perforation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics, with possible interval appendectomy
Intravenous antibiotics alone with no drainage
Urgent colonoscopy followed by discharge on oral antibiotics

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that for perforated appendicitis, usually associated with a longer 4-5 day history, an abscess should be managed with radiologic drainage and antibiotics for 14 days with possible interval appendectomy once inflammation has resolved. Upfront surgery is reserved mainly for failure of non-operative management. Antibiotics alone are appropriate for a phlegmon without an abscess, since there is nothing to drain.

optionExplanations.b: Upfront appendectomy in this setting is usually reserved for failure of non-operative management.
optionExplanations.c: Antibiotics alone are the strategy for a phlegmon without an abscess; a 6 cm collection should be drained.
optionExplanations.d: Hemicolectomy is not indicated for perforated appendicitis with a drainable abscess.
optionExplanations.e: Colonoscopy may be considered later, especially in patients over 50, to rule out a concurrent neoplasm, but it does not treat the abscess.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with known diverticular disease presents with generalized peritonitis. Blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg and heart rate 128 bpm despite fluids. Upright chest x-ray shows free air, and at urgent laparotomy there is feculent peritoneal contamination from a perforated sigmoid colon. Which operation is most appropriate?

options.text: Hartmann procedure with sigmoid resection, end colostomy, and closure of the rectal stump
Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage with drain placement and no resection
Sigmoid resection with primary anastomosis and no diversion
CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the pelvis
Elective sigmoid colectomy deferred for 6 weeks

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes gives Hinchey staging and treatment for diverticulitis: stage 3 is purulent peritonitis treated by resection or Hartmann procedure, and stage 4 is feculent peritonitis treated by Hartmann procedure. Surgery is indicated for an unstable patient with peritonitis or Hinchey stage 3-4 disease. The Hartmann procedure resects the diseased colon and creates a colostomy with a closed rectal stump, with colostomy reversal in 3-6 months.

optionExplanations.b: Laparoscopic lavage with drainage has been proposed for Hinchey stage 3, not for feculent peritonitis in an unstable patient.
optionExplanations.c: Resection with primary anastomosis plus a diverting loop ileostomy is an option for more stable patients, and an undiverted anastomosis in feculent contamination with shock is unsafe.
optionExplanations.d: Percutaneous drainage reduces the urgency of resection for abscesses but cannot treat established feculent peritonitis.
optionExplanations.e: Delaying operation is not an option in an unstable patient with free perforation; mortality of feculent peritonitis is about 35%.

source.reference: GS40 — Diverticulitis / Hinchey Staging and Treatment

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents with 3 months of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Hemoglobin is 92 g/L with a mean corpuscular volume of 74 fL and ferritin of 8 µg/L. He reports a recent positive fecal immunochemical test and looser stools. Physical examination and abdominal imaging are unremarkable. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Repeat fecal immunochemical test in 12 months

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that elderly persons presenting with iron-deficiency anemia should be investigated for colon cancer, and that case-finding in patients with suspicious symptoms such as a positive FIT, anemia, or a change in bowel habits is done with colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is also required to detect synchronous lesions, since flexible sigmoidoscopy is insufficient.

optionExplanations.b: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is explicitly insufficient because it cannot exclude synchronous proximal lesions.
optionExplanations.c: Repeating a screening test that is already positive delays diagnosis in a symptomatic anemic patient.
optionExplanations.d: Barium enema is a historical elective study and does not permit biopsy of a suspicious lesion.
optionExplanations.e: Capsule endoscopy is used for obscure bleeding when colonoscopy and endoscopy have already failed to identify a source.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman has 12 hours of constant severe right upper quadrant pain with nausea, anorexia, and a temperature of 38.2°C. There is inspiratory arrest on right subcostal palpation. White cell count is elevated with a left shift; bilirubin and lipase are normal. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a 6 mm gallbladder wall, and pericholecystic fluid. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Admission with hydration, analgesia, cefazolin, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours
Analgesia and rehydration with elective cholecystectomy arranged in 3 months
ERCP with sphincterotomy before any operation
Outpatient observation with oral analgesia alone

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes distinguishes biliary colic, treated with analgesia and elective cholecystectomy, from acute cholecystitis, treated with antibiotics and early cholecystectomy if surgical risk is appropriate. For uncomplicated cholecystitis cefazolin is recommended, and early cholecystectomy within 72 hours is preferred because it shortens hospitalisation and recovery with no benefit to delaying surgery. This woman has constant pain over 6 hours, fever, Murphy's sign, and sonographic wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid.

optionExplanations.b: Analgesia with elective cholecystectomy is the treatment of biliary colic, in which pain lasts less than 6 hours and there are no systemic or peritoneal findings.
optionExplanations.c: ERCP before surgery is indicated when common bile duct stones are present or suspected; her bilirubin is normal and the ultrasound shows no ductal stone.
optionExplanations.d: Percutaneous cholecystostomy is reserved for the critically ill or when general anesthetic is contraindicated.
optionExplanations.e: Acute cholecystitis requires admission, antibiotics, and definitive management rather than outpatient observation.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice. She is confused with a blood pressure of 84/48 mmHg. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are markedly elevated and lipase is normal. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. After fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics, what is the next best step?

options.text: ERCP with sphincterotomy for biliary decompression
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography with catheter drainage
Open common bile duct exploration with T-tube placement
MRCP to further define the biliary anatomy

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes acute cholangitis with Charcot's triad of fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice, and Reynolds' pentad when hypotension and altered mental status are added. Treatment is NPO, fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, and IV antibiotics, followed by biliary decompression, for which ERCP with sphincterotomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Elective cholecystectomy follows resolution of the acute episode.

optionExplanations.b: Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is used if ERCP is unavailable or unsuccessful.
optionExplanations.c: Cholecystectomy is recommended electively after the cholangitis resolves, not as the decompressive procedure in a septic patient.
optionExplanations.d: Open or laparoscopic duct exploration with a T-tube is reserved for failure of endoscopic and percutaneous decompression.
optionExplanations.e: MRCP is used when the diagnosis is unclear; here the obstructing stone is already demonstrated and decompression should not be delayed.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman notices a lump in her right breast. On examination there is a solitary 2 cm firm, rubbery, well-circumscribed, non-tender nodule that is freely mobile. It does not change appreciably with her menstrual cycle. Needle aspiration in clinic yields no fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Simple breast cyst from fibrocystic change

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes the fibroadenoma as the most common benign breast tumour in women under 30, presenting as a firm, rubbery, discrete, well-circumscribed, usually unilateral, non-tender, mobile, hormone-dependent nodule in which needle aspiration yields no fluid. All of these features are present in this young woman.

optionExplanations.b: Cysts of fibrocystic change vary with the menstrual cycle and yield fluid on aspiration.
optionExplanations.c: Fat necrosis follows trauma or breast surgery and is a firm, ill-defined mass often with skin or nipple retraction.
optionExplanations.d: A lipoma is a soft, mobile subcutaneous tumour rather than a firm rubbery discrete breast nodule.
optionExplanations.e: Intraductal papilloma most characteristically causes spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge.

source.reference: GS65 — Benign Breast Lesions / Proliferative Lesions Without Atypia

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with 10 hours of severe lower abdominal pain of acute onset, nausea, and anorexia. Temperature is 37.8°C and blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg. There is right lower quadrant tenderness with localized guarding. She is unsure of the date of her last menstrual period. Which investigation is indicated specifically because of her age and sex?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the tests to order in all patients presenting with an acute abdomen, and β-hCG is specified for women of childbearing age. This patient has severe abdominal pain of acute onset requiring urgent medical attention, and pregnancy must be excluded before further imaging or operative planning. The other listed tests are ordered for specific diagnoses rather than because of age and sex.

optionExplanations.a: Troponins are a key test when cardiac causes of abdominal pain such as MI are considered, not a sex-specific test.
optionExplanations.b: Lipase/amylase is the key test for suspected pancreatitis, ordered irrespective of sex.
optionExplanations.d: ALP, ALT, AST, and bilirubin are ordered when hepatobiliary pathology is suspected.
optionExplanations.e: Lactate is ordered to assess for ischemia and is not specific to women of childbearing age.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with 6 hours of painless bright red blood per rectum. He has no hematemesis or melena and the nasogastric aspirate is clear. Blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg after 1 L of crystalloid and hemoglobin is 108 g/L. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to detect and potentially stop the source of bleeding?
questions.explanation: Bright red blood per rectum with a clear nasogastric aspirate indicates a lower GI bleed, arising distal to the ligament of Treitz. Toronto Notes states that initial management of LGIB is colonoscopy to detect and potentially stop the source of bleeding, and that barium enema should NOT be performed if bleeding continues. Angiography or an RBC scan are used to determine the source as indicated once colonoscopy has not localized it.

optionExplanations.a: Barium enema should not be performed in ongoing lower GI bleeding.
optionExplanations.c: Angiography is used to determine the source as indicated, not as the initial test.
optionExplanations.d: Capsule endoscopy is reserved for obscure bleeding with no source found after colonoscopy and endoscopy.
optionExplanations.e: An RBC scan localizes but does not treat, and is used when colonoscopy has not identified the source.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man is on postoperative day 5 following a colon resection with a primary bowel anastomosis. He develops a temperature of 39.2°C with tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and abdominal pain. The wound looks clean and there is no crepitus. Which is the most likely cause of his postoperative fever?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes uses the timing of postoperative fever to identify the cause: fever on POD #3-7 is likely infectious, and the listed causes include UTI, surgical site infection, IV site/line infection, septic thrombophlebitis, and leakage at a bowel anastomosis, described as tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and abdominal pain. This patient's day 5 fever with exactly that constellation after a bowel anastomosis fits anastomotic leakage.

optionExplanations.a: Atelectasis causes fever on POD #1-2 and does not produce hypotension with abdominal pain.
optionExplanations.b: Malignant hyperthermia occurs hours after surgery, not on POD #5.
optionExplanations.d: Drug fever is a POD #8+ consideration and would not explain oliguria and abdominal pain.
optionExplanations.e: Reaction to blood products received during surgery causes fever on POD #1, not day 5.

questions.question: A 61-year-old asymptomatic man attends for a periodic health visit. He has a 35 pack-year smoking history and quit 4 years ago. Physical examination and spirometry are normal and he has no respiratory symptoms. According to the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care, which is the most appropriate lung cancer screening investigation?

options.text: Annual low-dose CT for up to 3 years

questions.explanation: The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health (2016) recommends screening with low-dose CT for high-risk patients only: age 55-74 yr, at least a 30 pack-year smoking history, and a current smoker or one who quit within the last 15 yr, with annual screening low-dose CT up to 3 yr. This man meets all three criteria, so annual low-dose CT is indicated.

optionExplanations.a: Chest x-ray is not the recommended screening modality for high-risk patients.
optionExplanations.c: Sputum cytology is not part of the recommended screening strategy.
optionExplanations.d: EBUS is used for diagnosis and staging of known lesions and for guided biopsies of lymph nodes and tumours, not for screening.
optionExplanations.e: He satisfies all of the high-risk criteria, so screening is recommended.

questions.question: A 25-year-old tall thin man who smokes develops sudden pleuritic left chest pain and dyspnea. He is tachypneic and tachycardic with blood pressure 76/48 mmHg. The trachea is deviated to the right, the left hemithorax is hyperresonant with diminished breath sounds, and neck veins are distended. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion
Simple aspiration of the pleural space
Chest tube insertion after a confirmatory CXR

questions.explanation: Contralateral tracheal deviation, hyperresonance, ipsilateral diminished breath sounds, and shock indicate a tension pneumothorax. Toronto Notes directs that for an unstable/tension pneumothorax the treatment is needle decompression then chest tube, with VATS bullectomy and pleurodesis reserved for when this is unsuccessful. Treatment must not be delayed for imaging.

optionExplanations.a: Observation plus O2 applies only to a stable, small (<3 cm), minimally symptomatic pneumothorax.
optionExplanations.c: Aspiration or chest tube is for the symptomatic or large but stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax, not for a patient in shock.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting for a confirmatory CXR delays decompression in a patient who is already hypotensive.
optionExplanations.e: VATS bullectomy and pleurodesis follow only if needle decompression and chest tube are unsuccessful.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with 12 years of GERD and Barrett's esophagus reports 3 months of progressive dysphagia, first to solids and now to liquids, with odynophagia, hoarseness, and 8 kg of weight loss. A barium swallow shows narrowing of the lower third of the esophagus. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is the most important risk factor for adenocarcinoma in the lower third of the esophagus, and progressive mechanical dysphagia to solids then liquids with weight loss is the classic presentation. Toronto Notes states that barium swallow showing narrowing is suggestive but not diagnostic, and that endoscopic biopsy is required to assess location, resectability, and confirm the diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: Repeating a test that is suggestive but not diagnostic delays tissue diagnosis in a patient with constitutional symptoms.
optionExplanations.c: Manometry assesses motility disorders and will not confirm carcinoma.
optionExplanations.d: CT contributes to staging but does not confirm the diagnosis, which requires biopsy.
optionExplanations.e: pH monitoring documents reflux but does not diagnose esophageal carcinoma.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man who had a gastrectomy 4 months ago describes episodes beginning about 20 minutes after eating: epigastric cramping, bloating, nausea, and emesis, together with dizziness, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Episodes are worst after sweetened drinks and settle within an hour. He is afebrile, is not jaundiced, and the abdomen is soft. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Early dumping syndrome occurs 15-30 min postprandially when rapid emptying of hyperosmotic chyme distends the jejunum and stimulates release of vasoactive hormones. Toronto Notes describes exactly this picture: postprandial epigastric cramping, bloating, emesis, nausea, and vasomotor symptoms of dizziness, palpitations, tachycardia, and diaphoresis. Treatment is frequent small meals high in fibre and protein and low in carbohydrates, avoiding liquids with meals.

optionExplanations.a: Afferent loop syndrome causes early postprandial distention with RUQ pain and bilious vomiting from obstruction of the afferent limb, without vasomotor symptoms.
optionExplanations.b: Alkaline reflux gastritis results from bilious duodenal contents refluxing into the stomach and does not cause postprandial vasomotor symptoms.
optionExplanations.d: Blind-loop syndrome from bacterial overgrowth presents with anemia, diarrhea, malnutrition, and hypocalcemia rather than discrete post-meal attacks.
optionExplanations.e: Postvagotomy diarrhea is caused by bile salts in the colon inhibiting water resorption and produces diarrhea, not postprandial cramping with palpitations.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman has a 12-hour history of a tender, irreducible 2 cm groin lump with overlying erythema. She has vomited once but continues to pass flatus and stool, her abdomen is soft and non-distended, and an abdominal x-ray shows no dilated bowel loops. Which type of hernia best explains the absence of obstructive findings?
questions.explanation: In a Richter's hernia only part of the bowel circumference, usually the antimesenteric border, is incarcerated or strangulated, so the lumen remains patent and the patient may not be obstructed. Toronto Notes warns that a strangulated Richter's hernia may self-reduce and thus be overlooked, leaving a gangrenous segment at risk of perforation in the absence of obstructive symptoms.

optionExplanations.a: In a sliding hernia part of the wall of the hernia sac is formed by a retroperitoneal structure, usually colon; it does not explain strangulation without obstruction.
optionExplanations.b: A pantaloon hernia is a combined direct and indirect hernia with peritoneum draped over the inferior epigastric vessels.
optionExplanations.c: Littre's hernia involves a Meckel's diverticulum within the sac.
optionExplanations.e: A Spigelian hernia is a ventral hernia through the linea semilunaris, not a groin hernia.

source.reference: GS34 — Abdominal Hernia: Classification and Complications

questions.question: A 71-year-old man presents with 5 days of progressive abdominal distention, obstipation, and colicky pain. He describes 3 months of narrowed stools and 7 kg of weight loss. Abdominal x-ray shows a dilated colon with a cut-off in the descending colon and CT confirms a large bowel obstruction. Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the top three causes of large bowel obstruction in order as cancer (60%), volvulus (10-15%), and diverticulitis (10%). Adenocarcinoma is an intramural cause of LBO, and this man's months of narrowed stools and weight loss preceding the obstruction point to an obstructing colonic malignancy. CEA should be drawn if malignancy is suspected.

optionExplanations.b: Volvulus accounts for only 10-15% of LBO and typically presents acutely without months of narrowed stools and weight loss.
optionExplanations.c: Diverticulitis causing edema and stricture accounts for about 10% of large bowel obstructions.
optionExplanations.d: An IBD stricture is an uncommon intramural cause and would usually follow a known history of inflammatory bowel disease.
optionExplanations.e: An extramural hernia containing sigmoid colon is an uncommon cause and would be evident as a groin mass.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man presents with tenesmus and bright red rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy and biopsy show an adenocarcinoma of the distal rectum, and MRI demonstrates involvement of the anal sphincter complex. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no distant spread. The surgeon determines that adequate distal margins cannot be obtained. Which operation is most appropriate?

options.text: Low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision
Proximal diversion with an ostomy alone

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that low anterior resection is the curative procedure of choice for rectal cancer if adequate distal margins of about 2 cm can be obtained, and that abdominoperineal resection is used if adequate distal margins cannot be obtained. APR involves removal of the distal sigmoid colon, rectum, and anus, and requires a permanent end colostomy.

optionExplanations.a: LAR requires adequate distal margins, which cannot be achieved here.
optionExplanations.c: TAMIS is local excision for select T1 or lesser lesions, polyps, or Tis that cannot be resected by colonoscopy.
optionExplanations.d: Colectomy with primary anastomosis is the usual operation for colon cancer, not for a sphincter-involving rectal tumour.
optionExplanations.e: Proximal diversion with an ostomy is a palliative procedure for obstruction, not a curative resection.

questions.question: An 82-year-old institutionalized man with chronic constipation presents with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, marked distention, and vomiting. He is afebrile with no peritoneal signs and a normal lactate. Abdominal x-ray shows a massively dilated loop with a coffee-bean sign whose central cleft points to the left lower quadrant. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Decompression by flexible sigmoidoscopy with insertion of a rectal tube
Right colectomy with ileotransverse colonic anastomosis
Observation with serial abdominal x-rays alone

questions.explanation: A coffee-bean sign whose central cleft points to the left lower quadrant indicates a sigmoid volvulus. Toronto Notes directs that sigmoid volvulus is managed by decompression with rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy and insertion of a rectal tube past the obstruction, with subsequent elective surgery recommended in medically fit patients because of a 50-70% recurrence rate. Urgent surgery is reserved for strangulation, perforation, or unsuccessful endoscopic decompression.

optionExplanations.b: Right colectomy with ileotransverse anastomosis is the operation for cecal volvulus, where the cleft points to the RLQ.
optionExplanations.c: Urgent surgery is indicated for strangulation, perforation, or failed endoscopic decompression, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: Non-operative decompression by barium enema is used for cecal volvulus discussions but carries a high perforation risk and is not the treatment of choice here.
optionExplanations.e: Observation alone leaves the closed-loop obstruction untreated.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has a 2-day history of right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, acholic stool, and fluctuating jaundice. She is afebrile with a normal white count. Bilirubin is mildly elevated with raised ALP and GGT, and lipase is normal. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct but no ductal stone. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Her fluctuating jaundice, acholic stool, dark urine, and cholestatic liver tests with a dilated duct suggest choledocholithiasis. Toronto Notes identifies MRCP as 90% sensitive and the non-invasive diagnostic test of choice, visualizing the ampullary region and the biliary and pancreatic anatomy. Proceeding directly to ERCP is reserved for a CBD stone seen on U/S, clinical ascending cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD, none of which she has.

optionExplanations.b: ERCP is diagnostic and therapeutic but invasive, with complications including ERCP pancreatitis; it is reserved for a visualized stone, cholangitis, or marked hyperbilirubinemia with a dilated duct.
optionExplanations.c: PTC is used for proximal bile duct obstruction or when ERCP fails or is not available.
optionExplanations.d: Delaying investigation risks cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.e: A HIDA scan is most useful for confirming a non-filling gallbladder in cholecystitis, not for CBD stones.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is admitted with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Lipase is markedly elevated and ALT is 210 IU/L. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones with no duct dilatation. She is treated with NPO, hydration, analgesia, and early enteral nutrition, and after 48 hours is afebrile, anicteric, and tolerating diet. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with a course of antibiotics

questions.explanation: An elevated ALT above 150 IU/L strongly suggests a gallstone etiology of pancreatitis, which accounts for 45% of acute pancreatitis. Toronto Notes states the stone often passes spontaneously and that cholecystectomy should be performed during the same admission, because 25-60% of patients have recurrence if no surgery is done.

optionExplanations.b: Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy is needed only if a CBD stone is impacted or there is cholangitis.
optionExplanations.c: Deferring surgery for months exposes her to a 25-60% recurrence risk.
optionExplanations.d: Drain placement and debridement are reserved for necrotizing pancreatitis refractory to medical management or sepsis.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics are not indicated for the initial diagnosis and are reserved for clear signs of infection on imaging.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man reports 2 months of jaundice, dark urine, steatorrhea, anorexia, and 9 kg of weight loss. Diabetes was diagnosed 3 months ago. On examination he is cachectic with a palpable, nontender, distended gallbladder. ALP and bilirubin are elevated and CA 19-9 is markedly raised. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ductal adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas
Adenocarcinoma of the body or tail of the pancreas

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that vague abdominal pain with weight loss plus jaundice in a patient over 50 yr is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise, and that pancreatic head tumours, which comprise 70% of cases, typically present with jaundice, steatorrhea, and weight loss along with anorexia, dark urine, cachexia, Courvoisier's sign, and recent onset DM. Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common type at 75-80%, and CA 19-9 is the most useful serum marker.

optionExplanations.b: Body or tail tumours account for 30%, tend to present later with weight loss and vague mid-epigastric pain, and fewer than 10% are jaundiced.
optionExplanations.c: IPMN is a distinct pathology and does not classically present with Courvoisier's sign and cachexia.
optionExplanations.d: Mucinous cystic neoplasm is an uncommon cystic lesion rather than the classic obstructing head mass.
optionExplanations.e: Pancreatic NETs are usually functional or non-functional lesions that do not typically produce this obstructive jaundice picture.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman whose menopause occurred at age 51 has completed breast conserving surgery and radiation for a 2.5 cm invasive carcinoma with two positive axillary nodes. The tumour is estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, and HER2 negative. She has no metastatic disease. Which adjuvant systemic agent is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Hormonal therapy is indicated for ER positive disease that is node-positive or high-risk node-negative. Toronto Notes specifies selective estrogen receptor modulators such as tamoxifen if premenopausal, or aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole if postmenopausal, for an optimal duration of 5-10 yr. This postmenopausal, ER positive, node-positive patient should receive an aromatase inhibitor.

optionExplanations.a: Tamoxifen is the SERM option chosen for premenopausal patients.
optionExplanations.c: Trastuzumab is added to chemotherapy for HER2 positive breast cancer; her tumour is HER2 negative.
optionExplanations.d: Goserelin achieves ovarian ablation, which is an option in premenopausal women.
optionExplanations.e: Progestins such as megestrol acetate are an alternative hormonal option, not first-line adjuvant therapy.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman has a 3 cm right adrenal mass discovered on CT performed for flank pain. On further questioning she describes episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis, and her blood pressure today is 172/98 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: AM aldosterone and AM plasma renin activity
FNA biopsy of the adrenal mass

questions.explanation: An adrenal mass greater than 1 cm found during investigation of unrelated symptoms is an incidentaloma and requires functional studies. Toronto Notes specifies plasma metanephrines, which are highly specific and sensitive, as the test for pheochromocytoma, with 24 h urine catecholamines if unavailable. Her episodic headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, and hypertension make pheochromocytoma the functional tumour to exclude first.

optionExplanations.b: The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test screens for Cushing's, which her symptoms do not suggest.
optionExplanations.c: AM aldosterone with plasma renin activity screens for an aldosteronoma, which typically presents with hypertension and hypokalemia rather than paroxysmal spells.
optionExplanations.d: FNA biopsy is not appropriate in most cases; diagnostic adrenalectomy by a high volume endocrine surgeon is preferred if there is diagnostic uncertainty.
optionExplanations.e: MRI is not as good as CT for adrenal masses and does not need to be done after CT.
